Lord Ashworth stood tall and inflexible before the solicitor's desk, his own face pale with a cold, rising anger. "You will explain yourself, Mr. Finchley. You _must_! I am not a boy to be scared by tales of goblins. What ghastly secret do you nurse that makes you speak so of my betrothed?"

"Ghastly secret-yes, that is the word for it! Ghastly secret-you have said it!"

"Does this concern my father's accident? Is it possible that Eleanor's family, the Pembertons, were involved in some way you have kept hidden?"

There was no answer. The old man shrank in his chair, his wrinkled hands shielding his eyes from the light.

"Is that it?" Ashworth persisted, his voice low and dangerous.

Finchley rose unsteadily to his feet, goaded, it seemed, by the relentless questioning into a final, frantic defence. "Let me be, Edward Ashworth," he rasped. "I have kept my counsel for eighteen years-do you truly believe you can break my will in a single afternoon? What right have you to demand anything of me? If you knew the whole truth you would know you have no rights at all-none-no right to the love of an honest woman-no right, if you must know, even to the name you bear!"

He froze then-aghast at his own words. Was the old man finally mad? Had the news of his engagement tipped his faithful servant into lunacy? In that terrible pause, a sharp rap upon the door, once ignored, sounded a second time. It was an intrusion from the world of sense and order, and both men seemed to grasp at it. Finchley sat down heavily; Lord Ashworth flung open the door. It was a young clerk with a telegram on a small tray.

"Well, man," Ashworth demanded brusquely. "What is it?"

"A wire for you, Mr. Finchley. From Dover, sir."

"I am not receiving messages," Finchley began, but then his eyes fell upon the envelope and he stopped. "Give it here," he said, his voice trembling. He tore it open at once.

"You may go, Thomas," he said to the clerk. He scanned the few typed words with a look of utter astonishment, which slowly gave way to something like dawning hope. The wire contained but a single sentence and a name: "ARRIVING CHARING CROSS TONIGHT. AURELIA."

"Edward," he said, turning to his master and holding out a trembling hand, "forgive me, if in my agitation I have said more than is proper. Grant me a little patience, and all will be made clear. The arrival of Aur-this person-is the one thing that could have happened to resolve this. You shall know everything soon."

"I am to believe, then," Lord Ashworth said icily, "that this stranger, this 'Aurelia', is to be your confidante; that she is to be made privy to my affairs-that her word is required before you can reveal a secret that touches upon the very honor of my name?"

"Precisely! You look angry and skeptical, but in time you will see. She is-she was once very close to our family. I can say no more. Go, Edward; trust me, believe me, neither your title nor your happiness shall be tarnished if I can help it. Cancel your appointment at the club; I will need you here this evening. To-morrow, if God is willing, this burden will be yours to share."

He bowed stiffly-confused, indignant, and went. What did it all mean? His life, until this point, had been a clear and sunlit path, without secrets or shadows of any kind. And now, suddenly, here were secrets and shadows in abundance. _What_ was this ghastly secret-_who_ was this mysterious Aurelia? He would have to wait until evening, it seemed, for the answer to both.

"One thing is certain as the stars," he muttered to himself as he descended the stairs, "I will not give up Eleanor, not for a thousand family secrets-not for all the mysterious women in Christendom! Whatever my father may have done, I at least have a clean conscience. The notion that the son must pay for the sins of the father is a barbaric one. Let the evening bring what it may, Eleanor Pemberton shall be my wife."

A CONFESSION.

"Mysterious, indeed!" he thought. "I wonder what her part is in this melodrama?" He bowed slightly as he passed; she inclined her head in a silent acknowledgment; then he made his way to the drawing-room to find Eleanor, to tell her that an unforeseen complication had arisen, and that their theatre engagement for the evening must be postponed. He was a poor actor, and the girl's clever grey eyes were very keen. She smiled as she watched him struggle for words.

You have been closeted with dear old Mr. Finchley; you have informed him that Eleanor Pemberton has agreed to become Lady Ashworth. You will appear before me one day and say: 'See here, Miss Pemberton, I am dreadfully sorry, you know, but it seems we have erred-_I_ have erred. "I don't know," Miss Pemberton replied coolly; "it might be for the best. Oh, do not look so thunderous, please-you know what I mean. I _am_ a nobody, as your circle reckons it. Mr. Finchley has been like a father to you; it is not worth the pain of breaking with him for my sake-I am not worth it. There are countless ladies in London, well-born, well-bred, and far prettier than I, who would be honored to accept your hand. Lord Ashworth, let us be friends and say farewell."

She held out her hand to him with a smile, proud and wonderfully serene. He snatched it with a cry, his grey eyes blazing, and pressed it to his lips.

Do not speak this way again, Eleanor; if you knew how your words wound me you would not have the heart for it, I know. Life can hold no sorrow for me half so bitter as the loss of you."

She listened with a kind of breathless wonder at his sudden passion, looking at him with wide, uncertain eyes.

"You love me so?" she whispered.

"A thousand times more than this. I would give my life for you, Eleanor. How foolish and trite it sounds, but, before Heaven, it is true."

She slipped her hand through his arm and held it fast.

"And I," she confessed, "feel as if I am in a dream from which I must soon awaken. It is all too beautiful to be real."

"I shall try," she promised.

The air within was warm and humid, thick with the scent of damp earth and strange, heavy blossoms. Great ferns uncurled in the corners, and orchids of impossible color and shape dripped from hanging baskets. It was a world unto itself--a tropical paradise incongruously attached to a stern English house. It was here, in this pocket of unreality, that reality, in its most unwelcome form, chose to find them.

A shadow fell across the glass-paned doorway. Both turned, startled out of their reverie. Standing there, silhouetted against the bright afternoon sun, was a figure, familiar and foreboding. He was a small, neat man, dressed in impeccable, somber black, his thin hair plastered precisely to his scalp. He held a leather portfolio under one arm.

"Finchley!" Ashworth exclaimed, his voice sharp with annoyance. The magical bubble had been burst.

Mr. Finchley stepped into the conservatory, his small, sharp eyes taking in the scene in a single, comprehensive glance: Lord Ashworth's proprietary hand on the young woman's arm; the young woman's flushed and startled face. A look of profound and sorrowful disapproval settled upon his features.

"I am occupied, Finchley, as you can see," Ashworth replied, his tone dangerously smooth. He made no move to release Eleanor's arm; if anything, his grip tightened in a gesture of defiance. "Miss Pemberton and I were enjoying the gardens."

Eleanor, mortified, tried to gently pull her hand away. "Mr. Finchley," she said, her voice regaining some of its former cool composure. "Lord Ashworth was being most kind. I should take my leave."

"You will do no such thing," Ashworth commanded, his voice low but absolute. He turned his full attention to the solicitor. "Whatever your business, Finchley, it can wait. This is neither the time nor the place."

"It is," she answered, her chin high.

"And is it not also a fact," Finchley continued, his voice taking on a methodical, relentless cadence, "that Pemberton Mills is, to use a term of art, financially embarrassed? That it is, in point of fact, teetering on the very brink of bankruptcy?"

"No," Eleanor whispered, her eyes fixed on the solicitor. "Let him continue."

Finchley nodded, a grim and unhappy victor. "Your father, Miss Pemberton, has spent the last six months seeking a substantial infusion of capital to save his business. A man I know to be a catastrophic financial risk comes begging for a loan. He has a daughter--a handsome, clever daughter. Do you imagine I could not see the shape of the trap being laid? I refused him on the spot. I told him Lord Ashworth's funds were not available for such speculative and doomed ventures, and I sent him away. I believed the matter was closed."

He paused, letting the silence in the warm, heavy air grow thick with his accusations.

"But I was wrong," he continued, his gaze returning to Eleanor with a sorrowful finality. "The father's direct approach failed. So a new, more subtle strategy was deployed. The daughter, by a most remarkable coincidence, finds herself employed in the very house where you are a guest. An acquaintance is struck. Sympathies are engaged. And now I find you here, in this conservatory, on the very verge of--of what, my lord? A proposal? A promise? An entanglement from which your honor will not permit you to retreat?"

Her own sudden employment with the Finches. It all fit together in a pattern of deceit she had been too innocent to see.

"It is not true," she whispered, her voice choked. She looked at Julian, her eyes wide with a desperate appeal. "Julian, you must believe me. I knew nothing. Nothing of the debts, of his visit to London--nothing!"

"I believe you," he said instantly, his voice ringing with conviction. He took a menacing step toward Finchley, his hands clenched into fists. "You have gone too far, Finchley. You will apologize to Miss Pemberton at once."

"Apologize?" The solicitor stood his ground, a small, stubborn rock against a tide of aristocratic fury. "I will do no such thing! I have spoken only the truth. It is a charitable interpretation, and one I should like to believe. But it does not change the facts! The fact is, her family is ruined. The fact is, any connection to them will result in scandal, financial importunity, and endless trouble. My lord, I implore you, think! Do not let a moment's infatuation destroy the honor and security of a name you have borne with distinction!"

"My honor," Ashworth said, his voice dropping to a dangerously low temperature, "is not your concern. It is my own. And it dictates that I stand by the woman I love, particularly when she is unjustly accused."

He turned his back on the solicitor, a gesture of ultimate dismissal, and went to Eleanor. She had backed away until she was pressed against the damp stone wall of the conservatory, her face buried in her hands. She was shaking.

"Eleanor," he said gently, trying to take her hands. "My darling, look at me."

She flinched away from his touch. "No! Don't touch me! He is right--can't you see? He is right! Perhaps I did not know it, but I am the bait in the trap all the same. My father's ruin--your fortune. Oh, it is too horrible!" A sob, torn from the very depths of her, broke free. "I thought my father kept a boarding house was bad enough," she said, a hysterical little laugh escaping her lips, referencing their earlier conversation. "But a ruined bankrupt? A schemer? Oh, how can I ever look you in the face again?"

"You will look me in the face now," he said, and with a gentleness that belied the strength in his hands, he pulled her hands away from her face and held them fast. His grey eyes, no longer blazing with anger, were filled with a profound and steady tenderness. "Eleanor Pemberton, I do not care if your father is a king or a beggar. I do not care if his factories coin money or stand in ruins. I asked you to be my wife--or I would have, if this meddling fool had not interrupted us. And I am asking you now. Will you marry me?"

Behind them, Mr. Finchley made a sound, a strangled gasp of disbelief and despair.

Eleanor stared at him, tears streaming unheeded down her cheeks. In the midst of her humiliation and horror, his proposal shone like a beacon. It was madness. It was impossible. It was the most wonderful thing she had ever heard.

"You cannot be serious," she whispered. "After this--after what you have heard--"

"What have I heard?" he countered, his grip on her hands tightening. "I have heard the gossip of a worried old man who sees plots in every shadow. I have heard that your father is in trouble, a fact which calls for compassion, not condemnation. And I have heard my own heart, which tells me that to lose you now would be a greater ruin than any bankruptcy. The world thinks I have everything, Eleanor. But without you, I have nothing. Nothing at all. Marry me. Let us face this together."

She searched his face, looking for any sign of doubt, of pity, of condescension. She found only love, fierce and unwavering. The last of her resistance washed away on a final tide of tears.

"Yes," she breathed, the word a bare whisper. "Oh, yes."

He let out a breath he had not realized he was holding and, ignoring the astounded solicitor completely, he gathered her into his arms. He held her as if he would never let her go, and for a long moment, the only sound in the humid air was the quiet weeping of a woman whose world had been shattered and then rebuilt, stronger than before, in the space of ten minutes.

Finally, Mr. Finchley spoke, his voice strained and thin. "My lord," he said, "have you taken leave of your senses?"

Ashworth slowly turned, his arm still securely around Eleanor's waist, holding her to his side. He looked at the solicitor, and for the first time, Finchley saw not the boy he had helped raise, but the master of the house, the Earl of Ashworth, in all his authority.

"On the contrary, Finchley," he said, his voice calm and resonant with a new power. "I believe I have just come to them. Miss Pemberton has done me the great honor of accepting my hand in marriage. You will be the first to offer your congratulations."

Do not let a moment's infatuation destroy the honor and security of a name you have borne with distinction!"

The landlord looked from the desperate, veiled lady to the earnest, pale-faced girl. He saw the genuine panic in their eyes. "I have a master key," he said, fumbling with a ring of keys attached to his belt. "But if he has bolted it from the inside..."

He selected a key and inserted it into the lock. It turned with a heavy click. He pushed the door. It opened a few inches and then stopped, blocked by something.

"It is bolted," he grunted, putting his shoulder to it. "Sir, are you all right in there? Sir!"

There was no answer but the groaning of the wood.

"Break it down," Inez ordered, her voice like a blade.

The landlord looked at her, then at the sturdy oak door. He took a few steps back, braced himself, and threw his full weight against it. The wood shuddered. He did it again. On the third attempt, there was a sharp crack of splintering wood and the door flew inward, revealing the room beyond.

It was a small, sparsely furnished chamber. A bed, a desk, a single chair. And on the floor, lying beside the desk in a heap of dark clothing, was Victor. He was deathly pale, his hair plastered to his forehead with rain and sweat. An overturned glass and a small, empty vial lay near his hand.

"Victor!" Inez screamed, a raw cry of a mother's ultimate terror. She rushed to his side, falling to her knees. "Oh, my son, my son! What have you done?"

Edith froze in the doorway, her blood turning to ice. The vial. The stillness of him. For one dreadful, unending second, she thought they were too late. Then she saw the faint, shallow rise and fall of his chest.

"He's breathing!" she cried, rushing forward. "He is alive! Landlord, fetch a doctor! Quickly!"

She knelt beside Inez, pushing the vial away with a trembling finger. She touched Victor's forehead. He was burning with fever. His lips were parted, and he muttered something, a slurred, broken phrase.

"The name... not my own... a sin... Edith..."

Inez was weeping, cradling his head in her lap, smoothing his damp hair. "He is alive," she whispered over and over, a prayer of thanks. "He is alive."

Edith looked at the man they both loved, lying broken and delirious on the floor of this sad, lonely room. Their quest was over. They had found him. But as she listened to his fevered, half-conscious words, she knew that the true ordeal, the unraveling of the terrible secret that had brought him to this pass, had only just begun.
